explanation: [[kw:Quartiles]] divide an ordered data set into four equal parts.
The [[kw:first quartile]] $ Q_1 $: about 25% of the data fall at or below this value.
The [[kw:second quartile]] $ Q_2 $: the median; about 50% fall at or below.
The [[kw:third quartile]] $ Q_3 $: about 75% fall at or below.
To find quartiles manually: order the data, find the median ($ Q_2 $), then find the median of the lower half ($ Q_1 $) and the median of the upper half ($ Q_3 $).
Technology may give slightly different quartile values due to different interpolation methods.

formulaCard.formula: $$Q_2 = \text{median of all data}$$ $$Q_1 = \text{median of lower half (values below } Q_2)$$ $$Q_3 = \text{median of upper half (values above } Q_2)$$
formulaCard.title: Finding Quartiles (Manual Method)

blocks.title: Quartiles

discoveryHook.scenario: A data set can be split into quarters. The first quartile marks the value below which 25% of the data fall, the second quartile is the median (50%), and the third quartile marks 75%. Quartiles help you quickly see how data are spread and where a particular value stands.

confusionCorner.body: Different software uses different formulas for quartiles, especially when $ n $ is not a multiple of 4. The values may differ slightly, but the interpretation is the same. [[imp:In this course, use the manual method unless told otherwise.]]
confusionCorner.title: Technology vs. Manual Quartiles

teacherCues: Write the nuclear power plant data on the board. Ask: 'After ordering, where would you split the data into four equal groups?'
Demonstrate that the median is Q2, then find the medians of the lower and upper halves for Q1 and Q3.

examples.prompt: The number of nuclear power plants in the top 15 countries: 7, 18, 11, 6, 59, 17, 18, 54, 104, 20, 31, 8, 10, 15, 19. Find $ Q_1, Q_2, Q_3 $.
steps: The median $ Q_2 $ is the 8th value: 18.
Lower half (7 values): 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 15, 17. Its median $ Q_1 = 10 $.
Upper half (7 values): 18, 19, 20, 31, 54, 59, 104. Its median $ Q_3 = 31 $.

steps: $ Q_1=10 $ means about 25% of these 15 countries have 10 or fewer nuclear power plants.
$ Q_2=18 $ means about half have 18 or fewer.
$ Q_3=31 $ means about 75% have 31 or fewer.
Together, they show the spread of the data.

steps: Median $ Q_2 $ is the 4th value: 25.

Upper half: 30, 34, 40 → median $ Q_3 = 34 $.

In an ordered data set of 15 values, about how many values lie below $ Q_1 $?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: About 25% of 15 ≈ 4 values, but practically 3 or 4. Answer: about 3 or 4. Accept 3.

Upper half of 7 values: after median 9, values 12, 15, 18; median of those is 15.

explanation: The [[kw:interquartile range (IQR)]] is the difference between the third and first quartiles: $ \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 $.
The IQR represents the range of the [[imp:middle 50%]] of the data and is resistant to outliers.
To identify [[kw:outliers]], compute [[imp:fences]]: Lower fence $ = Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR} $; Upper fence $ = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR} $.
Any data value below the lower fence or above the upper fence is considered an outlier.

visuals.title: Outlier Check for Nuclear Power Plant Data

legend.meaning: a constant used to define outlier boundaries

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$$ $$\text{Lower fence} = Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$$ $$\text{Upper fence} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$$
formulaCard.title: IQR and Outlier Formulas

confusionCorner.body: An outlier is a data point that lies far from the others, but it may be a valid observation. [[imp:Investigate the cause before removing it.]] It could represent an important extreme case or a measurement mistake.
confusionCorner.title: Outlier Does Not Mean Error

examples.prompt: For the nuclear plant data, $ Q_1=10 $, $ Q_3=31 $. Find the IQR and determine if 104 is an outlier.
steps: $ 1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 1.5 \times 21 = 31.5 $.
104 is above the upper fence, so it is an [[kw:outlier]].
examples.title: Example A – Finding IQR and Checking Outliers

examples.prompt: Explain to a partner why we multiply the IQR by 1.5 to set outlier boundaries, rather than just using the range.
steps: The range only uses the two extreme values, so a single outlier can stretch it enormously.
The IQR uses the middle 50%, which is unaffected by extremes.
Multiplying by 1.5 creates a reasonable 'fence' that is based on the spread of the bulk of the data.
This rule is a commonly accepted convention in statistics.
examples.title: Example B – Why 1.5?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back…

Explain to a partner: How does using IQR instead of range make outlier detection more robust?

examples.title: Example C – Check for Outliers
examples.prompt: Data: 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 35. $ Q_1=9 $, $ Q_3=13 $. Determine if 35 is an outlier.
steps: Upper fence $ = 13 + 6 = 19 $.
35 > 19, so 35 is an outlier.

discoveryHook.scenario: The range is sensitive to extreme values. The interquartile range (IQR) focuses on the middle 50% of data, giving a more resistant measure of spread. It also helps flag possible outliers using the 1.5 × IQR rule.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: The five-number summary includes the minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum.

discoveryHook.scenario: A box-and-whisker plot (boxplot) is a compact graph that shows the five-number summary at a glance: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. It reveals the center, spread, and skewness of a distribution without plotting every data point.

legend.meaning: Box from Q1 to Q3, line at Q2, whiskers to Min and Max.

explanation: A [[kw:box-and-whisker plot]] (boxplot) is a graphical summary of data based on the five-number summary.
The [[kw:five-number summary]] consists of: minimum, $ Q_1 $, median ($ Q_2 $), $ Q_3 $, maximum.

To draw: (1) Create a horizontal scale. (2) Plot the five numbers as points. (3) Draw a box from $ Q_1 $ to $ Q_3 $ with a vertical line at the median. (4) Draw whiskers from the box to the min and max.
The box shows the [[imp:middle 50%]] of the data; the whiskers show the lower and upper 25%.
The shape of the boxplot indicates skewness: a longer whisker on the right suggests right skew.

steps: Draw a horizontal axis covering the range 0 to 110.
Plot points at 6, 10, 18, 31, and 104 above the axis.
Draw a box from 10 to 31 with a vertical line at 18.
Draw left whisker from 10 to 6; right whisker from 31 to 104.
The long right whisker indicates a right‑skewed distribution.

Example B – Interpreting Boxplot

steps: The box length (IQR) shows the spread of the middle 50%.
A longer right whisker suggests the data are skewed to the right.
A longer left whisker suggests left skew.
If whiskers are roughly equal, the distribution is more symmetric.

steps: Median (Q2)=8; lower half (3,5,7) → Q1=5; upper half (9,12,14) → Q3=12.
Five‑number: 3, 5, 8, 12, 14.

confusionCorner.title: Whiskers Can End at Non-Outlier Extremes
confusionCorner.body: In a standard boxplot, whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values that are not outliers. If outliers are present, they are plotted individually, and the whiskers stop at the smallest/largest non-outlier values. [[imp:Our examples here show the basic version; later you'll see modified boxplots.]]

teacherCues: List the five-number summary for the nuclear plant data on the board. Draw a horizontal scale and construct the boxplot step by step.
Point out that the box spans Q1 to Q3, the line inside is the median, and the whiskers extend to the min and max (excluding outliers).

discoveryHook.scenario: Percentiles are everywhere: test scores, baby growth charts, income comparisons. The 60th percentile means you scored better than 60% of the group. Other fractiles like deciles (tenths) further divide data for finer comparisons.

blocks.title: Percentiles and Other Fractiles

steps: The 62nd percentile corresponds to a score of 1600.
This means approximately 62% of students scored 1600 or lower.
It does not mean the student got 62% of the questions correct.
examples.prompt: An ogive shows that the 62nd percentile of SAT scores is 1600. Interpret this.
examples.title: Example A – Interpreting Percentiles

steps: Scoring 80% means you answered 80% of questions correctly.
The 80th percentile means you scored higher than 80% of the test takers.
If the test was very hard, 60% correct might be the 80th percentile because most people scored lower.
Percentile describes relative standing, not absolute performance.
examples.prompt: Explain to a partner the difference between scoring in the 80th percentile and scoring 80% on a test.
examples.title: Example B – Percentile vs. Percent Correct
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back…

Explain to a partner: If the test is very hard and you score 60%, could you still be in a high percentile? Why?

steps: Number of scores less than yours = 15 (since 4 are higher, yours is 5th highest).
Percentile rank $ \approx (15/20) \times 100 = 75 $.
You are approximately at the 75th percentile.

teacherCues: Ask: 'If you scored in the 90th percentile on a test, what does that mean?' Then explain the difference between percentiles and percent correct.
Show the relationship: Q1 = 25th percentile, median = 50th percentile, Q3 = 75th percentile.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Percentile rank of } x = \frac{\text{Number of values less than } x}{n} \times 100$$
formulaCard.title: Percentile Rank Formula

explanation: [[kw:Percentiles]] divide an ordered data set into 100 equal parts. The $ k $th percentile $ P_k $ is the value below which $ k\% $ of the data fall.
[[kw:Deciles]] divide the data into 10 equal parts ($ D_1, D_2, \dots, D_9 $).
Percentiles can be read from a cumulative relative frequency graph (ogive).
A high percentile (e.g., 95th) indicates an unusually high value; a low percentile (e.g., 5th) indicates an unusually low value.

confusionCorner.body: A common mistake is confusing percentile with percentage score. A percentile tells how you compare to others; a percent tells how many items you got right. [[imp:Always check whether the number is a percentile rank or a raw percentage.]]
confusionCorner.title: Percentile ≠ Percent Correct

teacherCues: Write the z-score formula on the board: z = (x – μ)/σ. Ask: 'Why would we want to convert to z‑scores?'
Demonstrate that z = 0 means the value equals the mean, positive z means above the mean, negative z means below.

questions.prompt: The formula for a z‑score is $ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} $. Here, $ \sigma $ represents the population ___.
hints: It's the denominator in the z‑score.

questions.prompt: If μ = 100, σ = 15, and x = 130, what is the z‑score?
A z‑score of –1.8 is considered usual or unusual? (Assume bell‑shaped distribution.)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: A z‑score of –1.8 is within ±2, so it is not considered unusual.

visuals.title: z‑Score Examples for Vehicle Speeds (μ=56 mph, σ=4 mph)

legend.meaning: population standard deviation (use $ s $ for sample)

explanation: The [[kw:standard score]] or [[kw:z‑score]] measures how many standard deviations a data value $ x $ is from the mean $ \mu $.
Formula: $ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} $ (population) or $ z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s} $ (sample).
A positive z‑score: $ x $ is above the mean. Negative: below. Zero: equal to the mean.
z‑scores allow comparison of values from different data sets with different units or scales.
For bell‑shaped distributions, about 95% of z‑scores lie between –2 and 2. A z‑score beyond ±2 is [[imp:unusual]]; beyond ±3 is [[imp:very unusual]].

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Standard Score (z‑Score) and Comparing Positions

discoveryHook.scenario: You scored 85 on a math test and 90 on a history test. Which is better? Without knowing the class means and standard deviations, you can't tell. The z‑score converts both to a common scale, revealing how far each is from its mean in standard deviation units.

examples.prompt: Speeds: μ = 56 mph, σ = 4 mph. Find z‑scores for 62 mph, 47 mph, 56 mph. Identify any unusual speeds.
examples.title: Example A – Computing z‑Scores
steps: 62 mph: $ z = (62 - 56)/4 = 1.5 $. Not unusual (within ±2).
47 mph: $ z = (47 - 56)/4 = -2.25 $. This is less than –2, so unusually slow.
56 mph: $ z = 0 $. Exactly at the mean.

examples.title: Example B – Comparing Oscar Winners
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back…

Explain to a partner: Why does a more negative z‑score mean a younger relative age?
steps: Ledger's z‑score is further from zero (more negative), so he was more unusually young for his category.
Both are within –2, so neither is statistically unusual.
examples.prompt: Heath Ledger (age 29) for Best Supporting Actor (μ=49.5, σ=13.8); Penelope Cruz (age 34) for Best Supporting Actress (μ=39.9, σ=14.0). Who was more unusual relative to their category?

examples.title: Example C – Are These Unusual?
examples.prompt: A test has μ = 70, σ = 10. Find z‑scores for scores of 95 and 45. Are they unusual?
steps: Both lie beyond 2 standard deviations from the mean.

confusionCorner.body: A z‑score is a pure number, free of the original measurement units. This is why it can compare apples and oranges — or movie actor ages and vehicle speeds — on a common scale. [[imp:Think of z as the distance from the mean in 'standard deviation' steps.]]
confusionCorner.title: z‑Score Has No Units

presenterNotes: Block 1 (Quartiles): Emphasize the manual method for finding quartiles. Note that technology may give slightly different answers, but the concept is the same.
Block 2 (IQR and Outliers): The 1.5 IQR rule is a standard convention. Reinforce that outliers are not automatically errors—they may be important.
Block 3 (Boxplot): Draw the nuclear plant boxplot live. Highlight how skewness is visible from whisker lengths.
Block 4 (Percentiles): The difference between percentile and percent correct is a critical distinction. Use the ogive to read percentiles.
Block 5 (Blueprint/z‑Score): Tie everything together by showing how z‑scores, percentiles, and quartiles all describe position. The z‑score's unitless nature makes it a powerful comparison tool.
title: Measures of Position
